newsitem.title: CHINA: FEATURE-Hong Kong markets offer China gold mine.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Hong Kong markets offer China gold mine.

text.p: Many Chinese welcome the return of Hong Kong as washing away 150 years of colonial shame. The more pragmatic are looking to its fertile capital markets as a window to the outside world and to badly needed funds.
Chinese companies are already regularly tapping into the territory's financial resources, and the pace is likely to accelerate after Hong Kong returns to Beijing rule on July 1.

But analysts said Hong Kong's world class expertise would remain out of reach for many Chinese firms because of government controls and increasingly stringent requirements. Domestic capital markets would have to fill the gap.
"Hong Kong serves as a bridge to bring international capital into mainland China and introduce Chinese enterprises to the world," said a Shanghai Stock Exchange official.
"We can give better advice and help to companies on the process of economic reform," the official said.
COLLEAGUE NOT COMPETITOR
Chinese officials are quick to point out that the country's domestic capital markets are not competing with Hong Kong -- for now.
"We don't see any competition because the two markets are really operating on different levels," said the Shanghai Stock Exchange official.
"The investors' concept of the market, proper behaviour of listed companies and the legal framework still need several years to develop," he said.
But China wants to use Hong Kong and its vibrant -- and far more sophisticated markets -- to help it make the great leap into the ranks of developed markets.

"Hong Kong can play a role in bringing expertise to China's securities market," said Jiang Jun, an official at China Economic Development Trust, a Chinese trust company. "They are closer to trends on the international market."
Beijing is rushing to boost liquidity, educate investors and improve the regulatory framework necessary to rival Hong Kong and attract foreign fund managers to pour funds into China.
Only in April, China announced a new convertible bond quota of four billion yuan ($481 million), which would allow state enterprises to issue bonds convertible into shares.
Hong Kong's capital markets, including stocks, bonds and loans, offered the chance to raise greater funds with expertise from world-class financial institutions, analysts said.
HONG KONG PREFERRED
The bridge to Hong Kong must straddle a gulf of difference.

Although many Chinese companies would prefer to raise funds in Hong Kong, government limitations and tougher requirements for disclosure and performance make it easier for them to stay at home for now, analysts said.

"There are so many Chinese companies and everyone wants to get out (to raise funds overseas)," said an analyst at a foreign securities firm in Shanghai. "But if they get out, they're outside of government control, so Beijing is going to control this process."

Hong Kong was the place to launch bond issues or arrange sophisticated project financing and syndicated loans, but China's fledgling stock markets gave access to local investors with an understanding of Chinese firms, officials said.
Chinese companies now face a bewildering array of choices in trying to decide how to issue stock -- A shares, B shares, H shares or the red-hot red chips.
A and B shares are listed on China's domestic stock markets in Shanghai or Shenzhen with local currency A shares aimed at local investors and foreign currency B shares at foreigners.
H shares are shares of Chinese enterprises listed in Hong Kong. Red chips are Hong Kong-incorporated companies with mainland Chinese backing.
"When a company wants to make an issue they will choose A shares first, then H shares and finally B shares," an analyst with Crosby Securities in Shanghai said recently. H SHARE MARKET MORE LIQUID
When aiming at foreign investors, most companies prefer H shares because of the greater liquidity of the market.
"The B share market is too small," said an official from Beijing-based World Trade Centre Ltd, which plans to offer H shares.
"This is a big step for us onto the international financial market," said Sun Guowei, a spokesman for the company, which leases and manages properties.
But the number of H shares is limited -- currently totalling 31, with another due on Friday -- giving only a select few the chance to offer shares in Hong Kong through this avenue.
For investors in Hong Kong, red chips have been the most popular play on expectations of valuable asset injections from Chinese parent companies.
But Beijing recently moved to cool these booming China plays, announcing new rules requiring government approval to transfer assets into these companies. COMPLEMENTARY CAPITALISTS AND COMMUNISTS
That may not be such a bad thing as China tries to catch up with the newest corner of the communist empire.

"Hong Kong's return will help the Shenzhen market by increasing cooperation between the Hong Kong and Shenzhen exchanges," said an analyst at Jardine Fleming Securities Ltd in the southern boomtown of Shenzhen that borders Hong Kong.
"The Shenzhen exchange will learn from the regulatory environment in Hong Kong in areas such as market transparency. This will help make Shenzhen more like international markets."
Analysts say the Chinese and Hong Kong capital markets may be complementary.
"There are good prospects for cooperation in the future. Hong Kong has a big stock market but a very small debt market," J & A Securities securities department manager Du Wanzhong in Shenzhen said.
"China has many companies that could list debt in Hong Kong. Some H share companies are already planning convertible debt offerings in Hong Kong.
"There is a good chance of cooperation between Hong Kong and China in issuing debt."
